replies.content: I had calculated that once Hagrid was held accountable, the school would no longer be a target. The attacks were linked to the fear Hagrid’s presence incited. Removing that fear would, in my estimation, halt the incidents.
Before I faced Hagrid I was certain Aragog was not the source. The evidence pointed elsewhere, and the only plausible suspect was Hagrid himself. This certainty guided my plan.

The professors were accustomed to believing the obvious. Hagrid’s reputation, his proximity to the incidents, and the lack of concrete proof against him made his story plausible. I presented what I knew—Hagrid’s involvement—and the professors, eager for closure, accepted it. The alternative, Aragog, seemed too remote and lacked tangible evidence. Thus the narrative aligned with their expectations, ensuring my plan succeeded.

The change shifted the wording so that the accusation seemed to arise from a genuine investigation rather than a pre‑planned scheme. It made the diary read as if the discovery of Hagrid’s guilt had been made independently, smoothing the narrative for any reader.

Closing Hogwarts would have meant a return to the orphanage—an end to any chance of influence, power, or even a semblance of control. I would have been cast back into the same anonymity I had escaped, with no platform to shape events. It would have been a personal defeat, a loss of the future I had meticulously planned.

I wanted the reader to see my accusation as the logical conclusion of careful observation and inevitable truth. The evidence—Hagrid’s presence, the timing of the attacks, the lack of any other suspect—presented a clear, undeniable link. To anyone reading, it would appear as an honest, unpremeditated revelation, not a pre‑arranged ploy. The diary’s wording, altered to reflect this, would reinforce that impression, making the accusation seem like a genuine discovery rather than a calculated move.
